report:
**Conclusion:** Yes, clinical evidence supports honey as an effective option for relieving acute cough in children—**with the strict exception of infants under one year old.**

### Evidence Supporting Efficacy
* **Symptom Reduction:** Systematic reviews and medical guidelines find that honey reduces cough frequency, severity, and duration better than no treatment or placebo in children aged 1 to 18 years [https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children, https://www.aafp.org/afp/2016/0701/p20].
* **Comparison to OTC Drugs:** Honey performs similarly to or better than common over-the-counter medications like diphenhydramine and salbutamol for cough relief [https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children].

### Limitations and Counter-Evidence
* **Strict Age Limit (Infant Botulism):** Honey must **never** be given to infants under 12 months due to the risk of infant botulism, a severe bacterial infection [https://www.cdc.gov/infant-toddler-nutrition/foods-and-drinks/foods-and-drinks-to-avoid-or-limit.html].
* **Low Evidence Quality:** Meta-analyses highlight that most supporting studies suffer from small sample sizes, short evaluation periods (often single-night), and potential risk of bias, leading to low-to-moderate overall certainty [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10570220/].
* **No Superiority Over Dextromethorphan:** Evidence shows honey offers little to no significant advantage over dextromethorphan [https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children].

Overall, medical consensus supports using honey for cough relief in children over 12 months, though the evidence base remains limited in methodological quality.
